questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: In no way does this decision reflect a lack of confidence in the team.
In no way this decision reflects a lack of confidence in the team.
In no way reflects this decision does a lack of confidence in the team.
In no way this decision does reflect a lack of confidence in the team.
questions.explanation: 'In no way' triggers inversion: 'does this decision reflect a lack of confidence.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The policy stipulates that every employee undergo annual training.
The policy stipulates that every employee undergoes annual training.
The policy stipulates that every employee will undergo annual training.
The policy stipulates that every employee undergoing annual training.
questions.explanation: After 'stipulate that', formal English uses the subjunctive: 'every employee undergo annual training.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Had they foreseen the downturn, they would have hedged their exposure.
Had they foreseen the downturn, they will have hedged their exposure.
They had foreseen the downturn, they would have hedged their exposure.
Had they foresee the downturn, they would have hedged their exposure.
questions.explanation: 'Had + subject + past participle' is an inverted third conditional: 'Had they foreseen the downturn, they would have hedged...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The delays notwithstanding, the project delivered strong returns.
The delays notwithstanding of, the project delivered strong returns.
Notwithstanding the delays, but the project delivered strong returns.
The delays notwithstanding that, the project delivered strong returns.
questions.explanation: 'Notwithstanding' can also follow the noun it modifies: 'The delays notwithstanding, the project delivered strong returns.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: What is striking is how quickly the sector has recovered.
What striking is is how quickly the sector has recovered.
What is striking that is how quickly the sector has recovered.
What is striking is how quickly the sector recovering has.
questions.explanation: A 'what' cleft emphasizes a notable observation: 'What is striking is how quickly the sector has recovered.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The union disputes that productivity has genuinely improved.
The union disputes to that productivity has genuinely improved.
The union disputes productivity improving genuinely that.
The union is dispute that productivity has genuinely improved.
questions.explanation: 'Dispute' is followed by 'that + clause': 'disputes that productivity has genuinely improved.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Bearing in mind the current climate, caution is advisable.
Bear in mind the current climate, caution is advisable.
Borne in mind the current climate, caution is advisable.
Bearing in the mind current climate, caution is advisable.
questions.explanation: 'Bearing in mind' introduces a consideration: 'Bearing in mind the current climate, caution is advisable.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Countless startups has failed to secure a second funding round.
Countless startups have failed to secure a second funding round.
A countless startups have failed to secure a second funding round.
Countless startup have failed to secure a second funding round.
questions.explanation: 'Countless' + plural noun takes a plural verb: 'countless startups have failed.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The company ought to have disclosed the risk earlier.
The company ought to disclosed the risk earlier.
The company ought to have disclose the risk earlier.
The company ought to have disclosing the risk earlier.
questions.explanation: 'Ought to have + past participle' expresses a missed obligation: 'ought to have disclosed the risk earlier.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Scarcely had the ink dried when the deal fell apart.
Scarcely the ink had dried when the deal fell apart.
Scarcely had the ink dried than the deal fell apart.
Scarcely did the ink dry when the deal had fallen apart.
questions.explanation: 'Scarcely' at the start triggers inversion and pairs with 'when': 'Scarcely had the ink dried when the deal fell apart.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The merger talks have apparently stalled over valuation.
The merger talks have apparent stalled over valuation.
The merger talks apparently have stalled over valuation it.
The merger talks have stalled apparently over valuation, that.
questions.explanation: 'Apparently' hedges a claim and sits after the auxiliary: 'have apparently stalled over valuation.'

questions.topic: Advanced relative clauses (the way in which)
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The report criticizes the way in which the funds were allocated.
The report criticizes the way which the funds were allocated in.
The report criticizes the way in that the funds were allocated.
The report criticizes in the way which the funds were allocated.
questions.explanation: 'The way in which' is a formal relative structure: 'the way in which the funds were allocated.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Not for a moment did the analysts doubt the forecast.
Not for a moment the analysts doubted the forecast.
Not for a moment the analysts did doubt the forecast.
Not for a moment did doubt the analysts the forecast.
questions.explanation: Fronting 'not for a moment' triggers inversion: 'Not for a moment did the analysts doubt the forecast.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The restructuring of the division reduced overall costs.
The restructure of the division reduced overall costs.
The restructuring of the division reduce overall costs.
The restructuring the division reduced overall costs.
questions.explanation: Formal writing nominalizes verbs: 'restructure' becomes 'the restructuring of...'

questions.topic: Passive with modal perfect (ought to have been)
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The contract terms ought to have been reviewed more carefully.
The contract terms ought to been reviewed more carefully.
The contract terms ought to have review more carefully.
The contract terms ought to have being reviewed more carefully.
questions.explanation: Modal perfect passive: modal + have been + past participle: 'ought to have been reviewed.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: One factory increased output; the other, cut it.
One factory increased output; the other increased, cut it.
One factory increased output; the other is cut it.
One factory increased output; the other cuts it already.
questions.explanation: Ellipsis omits the repeated verb after a semicolon: 'the other, cut it' (= the other factory cut output).

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Growth is concentrated in one sector. That is to say, tech dominates.
Growth is concentrated in one sector, that is to say tech dominates.
Growth is concentrated in one sector. That is to say tech dominates.
Growth is concentrated in one sector that is to say, tech dominates.
questions.explanation: 'That is to say' begins a new sentence and is followed by a comma.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: For all its faults, the system has served the industry well.
For all of its faults, the system has served the industry well, that.
For all its faults, but the system has served the industry well.
All its faults for, the system has served the industry well.
questions.explanation: 'For all its faults' is a fixed concessive phrase meaning 'despite its faults': 'For all its faults, the system has served...'

questions.question: Which is the most appropriate formal opening line for an email requesting clarification on contract terms?
options: I am writing to seek clarification on several clauses within the contract.
Can you explain what this contract even means?
I am writing to seek clarification on several clauses within the contract, cheers.
This contract is confusing, please clarify asap.
questions.explanation: 'I am writing to seek clarification on...' is a standard formal request for clarification.

questions.question: Which is the most appropriate opening line for a formal complaint about substandard workmanship?
options: I am writing to formally register my dissatisfaction with the quality of the work carried out.
The work was shoddy and I'm not paying full price.
I am writing to formally register my dissatisfaction with the quality of the work carried out, honestly.
This workmanship is terrible, plain and simple.
questions.explanation: Formal complaints use precise, measured language such as 'I am writing to formally register my dissatisfaction with...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I am writing to chase up the outstanding invoice from last month.
I am writing to chase the outstanding invoice up of from last month.
I am writing to chase up of the outstanding invoice from last month.
I am writing to chase the outstanding invoice of up from last month.
questions.explanation: 'Chase up' means 'to follow up on something overdue': 'chase up the outstanding invoice.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Investigators found the accounts poorly maintained.
Investigators found the accounts poorly maintain.
Investigators found maintained the accounts poorly.
Investigators found the accounts poorly maintaining.
questions.explanation: 'Find + object + past participle' describes a discovered state: 'found the accounts poorly maintained.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Taking everything into account, the offer seems reasonable.
Take everything into account, the offer seems reasonable.
Taken everything into account, the offer seems reasonable.
Taking everything into account that, the offer seems reasonable.
questions.explanation: 'Taking everything into account' is a fixed absolute participle phrase meaning 'considering everything.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: In the interest of fairness, all bids were reviewed equally.
In interest of fairness, all bids were reviewed equally.
In the interest for fairness, all bids were reviewed equally.
Interest of the fairness, all bids were reviewed equally.
questions.explanation: 'In the interest of' means 'for the benefit of': 'In the interest of fairness, all bids were reviewed...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The rare vintage commands a considerable premium at auction.
The rare vintage orders a considerable premium at auction.
The rare vintage commands of a considerable premium at auction.
The rare vintage makes command a considerable premium at auction.
questions.explanation: 'Command a premium' is a fixed collocation: 'the rare vintage commands a considerable premium.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The committee has thoroughly reviewed the proposal.
The committee has reviewed thoroughly the proposal.
Thoroughly the committee has reviewed the proposal.
The committee thoroughly has reviewed the proposal.
questions.explanation: Adverbs of manner typically follow the auxiliary verb: 'has thoroughly reviewed.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Urban rents have soared. Conversely, rural prices have stagnated.
Urban rents have soared, conversely rural prices have stagnated.
Urban rents have soared. Conversely rural prices have stagnated.
Urban rents have soared conversely, rural prices have stagnated.
questions.explanation: 'Conversely' begins a new sentence and is followed by a comma.

questions.question: Choose the correct question tag.
options: The panel would seldom question such a respected expert, would it?
The panel would seldom question such a respected expert, wouldn't it?
The panel would seldom question such a respected expert, doesn't it?
The panel would seldom question such a respected expert, does it?
questions.explanation: 'Seldom' makes the statement effectively negative, so the tag is positive: 'would seldom question..., would it?'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The pilot scheme was not entirely successful.
The pilot scheme was not all successful entirely.
The pilot scheme not was entirely successful.
The pilot scheme was entirely not successful.
questions.explanation: Formal understatement places 'not' before the adverb: 'was not entirely successful.'

questions.topic: Advanced conditionals (Had it not been for)
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Had it not been for a last-minute investor, the venture would have folded.
Had it not for a last-minute investor, the venture would have folded.
Had it not been the last-minute investor, the venture would have folded.
Had it not been for a last-minute investor, the venture will have folded.
questions.explanation: 'Had it not been for' means 'if it hadn't been for': 'Had it not been for a last-minute investor, the venture would have folded.'
